extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical mechanics; scholars studying Newtonian dynamics
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook-style exposition and critique of Newton's principal contributions to mechanics (concepts of force, mass, composition of forces, and action–reaction), including methodological rules for natural inquiry and illustrative experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule I (Regulae Philosophandi)
rubrics_metrics.description: "No more causes of natural things are to be admitted than such as truly exist and are sufficient to explain the phenomena of these things."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton's first rule prescribes parsimony in explanatory causes: admit only those causes that truly exist and suffice to explain observed phenomena. Use this to avoid introducing unnecessary hypothetical causes when accounting for experimental results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule II (Regulae Philosophandi)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Therefore, to natural effects of the same kind we must, as far as possible, assign the same causes; e. g., to respiration in man and animals; to the descent of stones in Europe and in America; to the light of our kitchen fire and of the sun; to the reflection of light on the earth and on the planets."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply uniformity of cause: similar phenomena should be explained by the same causes where possible. This encourages generalization and consistency across contexts and experimental systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule III (Regulae Philosophandi)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Those qualities of bodies that can be neither increased nor diminished, and which are found to belong to all bodies within the reach of our experiments, are to be regarded as the universal qualities of all bodies."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat empirically invariable properties observed across experiments as universal qualities. This supports treating certain mechanical properties (e.g., aspects of mass/inertia under given conditions) as general features of bodies unless counter-evidence appears.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule IV (Regulae Philosophandi)
rubrics_metrics.description: "In experimental physics propositions collected by induction from phenomena are to be regarded either as accurately true or very nearly true, notwithstanding any contrary hypotheses, till other phenomena occur, by which they are made more accurate, or are rendered subject to exceptions."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regard inductive generalizations as provisionally true and practically reliable until contradicted by further observations; do not discard them merely for speculative hypotheses. Use experiments to refine or falsify such propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding speculative hypotheses — 'hypotheses non fingo'
rubrics_metrics.description: Newton's stated attitude: he 'does not frame hypotheses' and 'is not concerned with hypotheses as to the causes of phenomena, but simply wishes to express ... what is otherwise expressed in the description of the motion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological injunction to avoid positing causal explanations beyond what experiments justify. Focus on transforming and stating actual facts (phenomena) rather than inventing untested mechanisms; use differential/quantitative description rather than speculative cause-claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concept of mass as distinct from weight (inertia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass is a property distinct from weight that determines a body's resistance to change of velocity (inertia); this is illustrated by examples (fly-wheel resisting changes in motion, balanced wheel on axle still resisting motion changes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not define mass circularly (Newton's density×volume formulation is noted as unfortunate). Instead, understand mass operationally as the property that makes bodies resist changes in motion; identify it via experiments showing resistance to acceleration independent of gravitational weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measuring mass by weight under invariant g (pendulum experiments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Newton's demonstration: if gravitational acceleration g is the same for different materials at the same point (established via equal-period pendulums of equal length but different materials), then mass ratios can be measured by weight ratios (p = m g).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To equate mass and weight for measurement, verify experimentally that g is independent of chemical composition at the measurement location (e.g., equal pendulum periods with equal-size bobs of different materials, correcting for air resistance). Only then infer m ∝ weight p and use p = m g to determine masses comparatively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of composition of forces (parallelogram of forces)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a body is acted on simultaneously by two forces producing motions AB and AC in the same time interval, the resulting motion is AD; accelerations imparted by independent forces are measures of the forces, and the resultant corresponds to the diagonal of the parallelogram constructed on the component directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat forces as vectorially independent: represent forces by accelerations (or proportional path lengths in equal times) and compose them by parallelogram (vector addition). Ensure the assumption of independence of forces holds (without it the principle fails). Use proportionality to construct resultant magnitude/direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of action and reaction (equality of pressure and counter-pressure)
rubrics_metrics.description: A body that presses or pulls another body is pressed or pulled in exactly the same degree by that other body; pressure and counter-pressure (force and counter-force) are always equal and opposite. As measure of force Newton uses quantity of motion (momentum), implying equal and opposite momenta exchanged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply conservation of momentum/reciprocal interaction as a primary dynamical principle in solving mutual-action problems. Complement the principle with experimental corroboration (e.g., Wren's impact experiments, Newton's sealed-vessel magnet/iron in water) to confirm equal and opposite momenta exchange in collisions/contacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of experimental corroboration for dynamical principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Newton sought experimental corroboration of dynamical principles (e.g., action–reaction) and cites experiments by Wren and his own (sealed vessels with magnet and iron colliding in water) as support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on instinctive or purely philosophical arguments; design and conduct experiments to test dynamical assertions (impacts, mutual interactions in controlled setups). Use experiments to confirm both qualitative and quantitative consequences (e.g., equal and opposite momenta, velocity ratios inversely proportional to masses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative acceleration determines contact pressure (apparent weight)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contact pressure (apparent weight) depends on the relative acceleration between a load and its support: e.g., if a table falls with acceleration y, the pressure on it is m(g − y); if it rises with y the pressure is m(g + y); in free fall (y = g) pressure vanishes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing statical/kinematical problems in non-inertial frames or accelerated supports, compute apparent weight via p = m(g − y) (relative acceleration). Use this to predict pendulum periods under acceleration, effects demonstrated by Poggendorff's apparatus, and macroscopic phenomena like tides where relative accelerations determine mutual pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: System acceleration and 'moving force' (m φ) for connected masses
rubrics_metrics.description: For connected masses (e.g., mass M joined to mass m), the acceleration of the combined system under an external acceleration φ of one part is determined by the product m φ (called 'moving force') and the total mass M + m, yielding a_system = m φ /(M + m).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing composite/rigid systems or elastic connections, account for distribution of acceleration via the effective moving force m φ and total inertia. Use the relation a = m φ /(M + m) to compute the common acceleration, and be mindful of possible internal oscillatory motions which may be neglected if tensions/constraints prevent large amplitudes.
